chapter_theme: Ainkurunuru 11 to 20, the marutham reed decade of Orampokiyar: every poem opens on the reed (வேழம்) of the husband's ford-town, flowering like sugarcane, a horse's plume or a heron, serving as kohl tube or bathing float, and closes on the wife's body (shoulders, eyes, bangles, heart) bearing the cost of his other women.

11.reading: The wife says that, ashamed of the cruelty of the lord of the ford-town where the vayalai of the house-yard and the reed twine together, she keeps saying he is good, but her broad soft shoulders say he is not.
11.nuance: Her words and her body take opposite sides: shame (நாணி) makes her defend him, and the wasting shoulders give the verdict she will not. Line 1 can be read as the house creeper twining round the reed of the ford, the wife still holding to a man who belongs outside, but which plant clasps which is not fixed by the syntax, so it is left as scene, not iraicchi.

thinai_evidence.note: the reed of the watered ford and the ford-town lord fix the field land

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai for this decade; inferred from யாமே and என் தோளே: the wife speaks of her own shoulders

12.reading: The wife says: let the lord of the ford-town, where the reed on the bank flowers like sugarcane, keep up his cruelty as much as he likes; as for her, let her broad soft shoulders lose.
12.nuance: The optatives (ஆற்றுக தில்ல, தோற்கதில்ல) give up the contest rather than make it: she grants him his cruelty and her shoulders their defeat. The traditional reading of the worthless reed that flowers like the sugarcane as the other woman passing for the wife has only one clear correspondence and no stated other woman, so it is not tagged as ullurai.

13.reading: Of the lord of the cool ford, where the reeds of the north bank put out white flowers like the frothing plume of a fine horse, the speaker says that his women know no rest even at midnight, when the town sleeps.
13.nuance: The whole sense turns on துயல் in the last line: taken as துயில் (sleep) the lord's women lie awake while the town sleeps; taken as distress, they are untroubled, which would make the line sarcasm. The reed's white plume is set beside a war-horse's crest, a puram ornament on a field weed.

thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai for this decade; inferred and uncertain: பெண்டிர் may be the wives (the speaker among them) kept awake by his roving, or said in mockery of them

14.reading: The speaker says that the chest of the lord of the gem-clear ford, where the flag-flowered reed brushes the nearby mango with young fruit and its rich shoots sway, has a sweet softness that brings cool sleep.
14.nuance: The only poem of the decade with no complaint. The reed touching the young mango's shoots (வடுக்கொண் மாஅத்து வண்தளிர்) could hint at a man drawn to a young girl, but nothing in the poem states it, so it stays scene.

15.reading: The wife says that the lord of the old reed town, whose reed serves as a float and partner to the leaf-skirted women who bathe in the swelling flood, is lord of a town but not lord of her.
15.nuance: The pun ஊரன் ஆயினும் ஊரனல்லன் empties his title: he lords it over a town but is no husband. புனலாடு with a reed float is the marutham man's water-play with other women.

16.reading: The wife says that thinking of the lord of the flower-crowded town, where little girls pour collyrium into the hollow round stems of the tall-flowered reed, her kohl-lined eyes, once like flowers, are coated over with gold-pale pallor.
16.nuance: Two kohls meet: the girls fill the reed tubes with collyrium, and her own kohl eyes (உண்கண்) are covered over with gold, so the town's play with the reed is set against the ruin of her painted eyes.

17.reading: The wife says that since the lord of the town, where the white reed flower swaying on the bush looks like a heron flying in the sky, now desires new women, her simple heart has become empty.
17.nuance: The reed flower only looks like a flying heron, and the new women (புதுவோர்) are named in the next breath; the image of a showy look-alike fits them, but only one correspondence can be named, so it is a near miss for ullurai. மடங்கெழு, full of simplicity, makes her trust the cause of the emptiness.

18.reading: The wife says that the lord of the field-town, where the reed sways like sugarcane beside the serunthi that is like dark sedge, made her eyes, matched like paired flowers, weep when he left: did he not say he would never leave?
18.nuance: She quotes his own promise (பிரியலென்) against him: the question ends the poem on the broken word rather than on her grief.

19.reading: The speaker says that because he is lord of the town of cool groves, where the newly flowered great branch of the sandbank mango smells of lovers' bodies and the white reed's plume brushes there, her eyes, troubled, shed tears like flowers in the rain.
19.nuance: The grove itself smells of lovers (புணர்ந்தோர் மெய்ம்மணம்), so the town's very air tells her where he spends himself; ஊரன் ஆகலின், 'because he is that town's lord', makes the place the charge.

20.reading: The wife says that thinking of the lord of the town near the ford, where the six-legged fair-winged bee brushes the flowering of the hundred-petalled lotus and the hollow reed looks like bamboo, her bright bangles, once lovely on her wrist, loosen and slip away.
20.nuance: The bee working the many-petalled lotus is the traditional figure of the man among many women, but the poem states no other woman, only her thought of him, so it is scene. The bamboo, a hill thing, enters only as the measure of the reed.

links.note: In both the wife's shoulders waste and she will not call him cruel; in Ainkurunuru 11 she says he is good while her own shoulders say he is not, in Kural 1236 she is pained that others call him cruel because her shoulders and bangles slacken.
links.teaches: The Sangam poem sets the accusation inside her own body, against her own words, while Valluvar moves it to other people reading her body, so the couplet's defence of him against outsiders presupposes the older poem's private split between what she says and what her shoulders show.

links.note: The two poems share the refrain துறைகேழ் ஊரன் கொடுமை ... யாமே ... என் தடமென் தோளே; in 11 she calls him good and the shoulders contradict her, in 12 she lets him keep his cruelty and lets the shoulders lose.
links.teaches: Read in order, the shared refrain moves the wife from denial, where her body overrules her words, to surrender, where she grants him the cruelty and her body the defeat, so the decade builds a progression out of near-identical lines.

links.note: Ainkurunuru 15 has the wife say that the man whose town's reed is a float to the bathing women is no husband of hers; in Akananuru 186 the courtesan says their bond was only as far as bathing together on a float of reed (வேழத்துப் புணைதுணை யாகப் புனல்ஆடு கேண்மை).
links.teaches: The same reed float is the wife's proof that he belongs to other women and the courtesan's plea that the affair was mere water-play, so the pair shows the marutham reed raft as a contested sign whose meaning depends on which woman speaks.

links.note: Ainkurunuru 14 praises the chest of the ford-town lord for its softness that gives cool sleep; Naladiyar 389's wife of the field-town lord looks at the same chest smeared with sandal by other women's breasts.
links.teaches: The marutham husband's chest is the wife's place of rest in the Sangam poem and the evidence of his other women in the Naladiyar, so the later moralist turns the older image of comfort into the record of its betrayal.

links.note: In both the wife recalls that he promised not to leave (பிரியலென், அஞ்சல்) and then left; Ainkurunuru 18 ends on her weeping eyes and the question, Kural 1154 asks whether those who believed his assuring words are at fault.
links.teaches: The Sangam wife quotes his broken promise as an accusation, while Valluvar's wife turns it into a question of blame for having believed, so the couplet adds to the older scene a moral reckoning about trust that the poem leaves unasked.

links.note: In both the wife's bangles slip from her wrist because of the man; in Ainkurunuru 20 they loosen as she thinks of him, in Kural 1157 they broadcast that he has left.
links.teaches: The Sangam poem treats the slipping bangle as the private effect of memory, while Valluvar makes the same bangle a gossip that announces his desertion to everyone, so the couplet turns an inner sign into public scandal.

source_issues: 13: line 4 reads துயலறியலரே; if the word is துயில் (sleep) the lord's women lie awake, if துயல் (distress) the line is sarcasm; the sense turns on it.
14: line 3 reads மணித்துறை வீரன் where every other poem of the decade has ஊரன்; வீரன் may be a misreading of ஊரன் (not confirmed against another edition).
19: line 2 reads மெய்ம்மணங்க் கமழும், with a stray க் after the nasal, likely an e-text slip for மெய்ம்மணங் கமழும்.
11-20: the colophon gives no thurai for the decade (and the e-text no decade title), so every speaker in thurai_akam is inferred from the poem.
